blindSummary:
This state/province is the only sub-national unit in the country — and in its whole world region — to legislate the state of gender transition itself as a criminal offence. A provision of the religious-law bill passed in August 2026 makes it an offence for an adherent of the state religion to change their own gender, cause another person's gender to be changed, or induce someone to do so, punishable by a fine of up to 3,000 units of local currency, imprisonment up to two years, or both. The state/province had already brought its first prosecution of a trans woman under the predecessor 2019 religious-law ordinance, via an operation by its religious morality enforcement agency at a gathering of transgender individuals, heard at the state's religious court. Critically, the country's highest court struck down 16 of the 2019 ordinance's 18 provisions in February 2024 as outside state power; the state/provincial assembly resolved to re-enact them anyway, and did so in August 2026. That sequence demonstrates deliberate institutional commitment, not a stray provision.

This sits well below the country-wide average because the state/province adds a qualitative legal risk absent elsewhere: criminalisation of identity and existence themselves, not merely public-order or cross-dressing offences. The two-year imprisonment penalty and the completed prosecution set a precedent that other state/provinces compare against. A trans visitor who adheres to the state religion is squarely within jurisdiction; a non-adherent visitor is technically outside the religious courts but still exposed to the climate this creates. Compared with a neighbouring state/province whose hostility is expressed through official signboards and a stated intent to generate hatred but which has no criminal provision targeting gender transition as such, this one criminalises being trans itself.
